implementation_notes: Kotlin/JVM inherits Java's profiling (async-profiler, JFR) and its wins, and adds two Kotlin-specific ones: allocation of a lambda per call (a non-inline higher-order function allocates a Function object, so `map`/`filter`/`forEach` in a hot loop allocate per iteration unless the lambda is inlined - this is exactly why `inline` exists and why the stdlib marks withLock/let/run/apply inline), and boxing (a List<Int> boxes every element where IntArray does not). Kotlin also has its own collection overhead (Sequence adds iterator objects where a direct loop does not), so a Sequence in a hot loop costs allocations a plain loop does not. JMH with warm-up is the benchmark, exactly as in Java, because of JIT tiering.
idiom_name: async-profiler / JFR attribution plus JMH with warm-up; Kotlin wins are lambda-inlining (avoiding per-call allocation) and avoiding boxing
pitfalls: A non-inline higher-order function (map/filter/forEach/reduce) allocates a Function object per call in a hot loop; use an inline function or a plain loop.
Sequence adds iterator objects per stage where a direct loop does not - a Sequence in a hot loop allocates several times over.
List<Int> boxes every element; IntArray does not - and boxing is both an allocation and a pointer chase.
Benchmarking without @Warmup measures the JIT's interpreted tier, exactly as in Java.
Kotlin's stdlib data classes (data class Pair) allocate; on a hot path use primitives or reuse a mutable holder.
